gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'Belkin 40W Dual USB-C' charger ChatGPT showed delivers at most 20 W to any single port (Belkin: '40W total output (20W per port)'). A phone on it charges no faster than on the $5 onn 20W block, while the Anker 33W block gives 33 W to one USB-C device and drops to 20 W on USB-C once the USB-A port is also in use.
standout_why: I read three rival pages. whoahome.com/best/compact-usb-c-chargers says 'The watt figure on a charger is what one port gets when nothing else is plugged in', which the Belkin WCB006 contradicts, and the page doesn't cover the Belkin 40W Dual or the Anker 33W. laptopbee.com/best-30w-usb-c-chargers covers port splits only for UGREEN 3-Port and INIU; it doesn't mention the Belkin 40W Dual or Anker 323. The Tom's Hardware best-usb-chargers page came back truncated, so I couldn't check it. Android Authority returned 403 and the Guardian couldn't be fetched, so I couldn't check those either. Of the pages I could read, none normalises headline watts to watts per port, and none warns that a 40 W dual charger gives one phone 20 W.
decides: It knocks out the Belkin 40W Dual + cable card ($24.88 at Walmart in ChatGPT's answer) for anyone charging one phone or tablet. It gives the same 20 W as the $5 onn block, so its '40W' only pays off when two USB-C devices charge at once. For one device, a single-port block with the same headline rating gets the full figure, for example Belkin's 30W and 45W '+ USB-C Cable' bundles or the single-port retractables already on our page. The Anker 33W 2-port is fine for one phone (33 W on USB-C alone). I couldn't source the per-port split for the cable bundle (B2326), so the 20 W + 12 W shared figure applies only to the A2331 sold without a cable. The page's table should have a 'one device gets / two devices get' column, with the Belkin 40W Dual's 20 W as the footnote.
